units.label: 人类句子理解
units.description: 人类对GP/非GP结构及合理性/动词类型材料作限时问答，检验三种非互斥解释。

units.label: 语言模型句子理解
units.description: 固定模型与公开检查点在相同句问项目上输出答案概率，比较六条件并与人类关联。

units.label: 语言模型改写
units.description: 将同类句子拆成两句，检查格式、动词位置和潜在宾语是否被错误附着；不新增人类改写样本。

units.label: 图像生成理解验证
units.description: Dall-e-3生成句子图像，人工分四类，检查误解模式的跨任务一致性；没有同批人类图像任务。

units.label: 共享刺激构造与合理性预检
units.description: 使用既有和新增句框，GPT4合理性打分选取材料，并从Wikipedia估计动词及物倾向。

units.label: 统计与人机相似度分析
units.description: 用混合效应检验人类条件差异、词项相关和人机项目/条件两层秩相关。

facts.statement: 研究宾语/主语花园路径句的持续误解：后接名词短语先被当作前一动词宾语，最终结构却要求其为后一动词主语。提出三种非互斥解释：句法重分析困难、语义上可作宾语、可选及物动词寻求完整论元。

method_function.text: 由竞争解释指定句法、合理性和动词类型对照。

facts.statement: 45套可选及物动词材料（既有24套、新编21套）交叉GP/非GP与合理/不合理，另24套反身/非宾格动词材料（既有12套、新编12套）只在合理语境中变换GP/非GP。构成六条件，不能称完整2×2×2全因子。

method_function.text: 区分完全交叉子设计与动词类型的受限比较。

facts.statement: 附录报告并列出228个句子；45×4+24×2与此数一致。GP/非GP通过从句前后位置改变，合理性通过潜在宾语名词改变；附录保留完整原句，不以概括替代材料来源。

method_function.text: 保存最小对照的构造操作与句子层数量。

facts.statement: 用GPT4按1–7分评价合理性，只选择合理句评分至少比配对不合理句高3分的句对；这是材料预检，不是受测模型自己更新权重，也不等同独立人类合理性验证。

method_function.text: 以评分差阈值确保语义操纵。

facts.statement: 可选及物动词的transitivity bias用Wikipedia中及物用法占比估计，附录A列词项值；随后与理解正确率作相关，检验动词词汇倾向是否关联误读。未从这一计数步骤推断有训练解析器。

method_function.text: 引入连续词项特征作为解释变量。

facts.statement: 每句配置简单理解问题和针对错误宾语附着的GP问题。简单问题问主句事件，GP问题问是否发生误解析动作；二者分别测基本理解与目标误读。

method_function.text: 通过诊断性问题与基本理解参照区分任务失败。

facts.statement: 对可选及物句的GP问题，作者承认严格答案是Not necessarily：动作可能发生但不被句意蕴涵；实验仍将Yes记错、No记对。该二元标签是操作化约定，不表示事件客观不可能发生。

method_function.text: 固定理解评分标准并保留蕴涵与可能性的边界。

facts.statement: 通过Prolific招募英语母语者；每个456句问对呈现给10名参与者，每人两个练习后只做一个正式句问项目。456是句问对数，不是参与者数；正文未另给可核验的去重/排除后总人数表。

method_function.text: 记录人类样本分配单位和单trial设计。

facts.statement: 逐词呈现，每词400ms、词间空屏100ms；句后问题限5秒，超时计错。平均完成约1分50秒，补偿0.30英镑并报告时薪9.64英镑，获大学伦理批准。限时和超时规则是计分组成部分。

method_function.text: 控制呈现节奏及反应窗口。

facts.statement: 作者采用每人单个正式trial以减少疲劳与学习效应，而非反复测同一人的六条件。文中没有报告独立实验来证明疲劳/学习被完全消除。

method_function.text: 以设计降低跨trial学习和疲劳。

facts.statement: 模型few-shot例子包含句子、问题和正确答案，不含GP结构；每模型使用两种system提示×四种例子顺序，共8种提示，分别提取正确和错误答案token概率后平均。不能把8种提示称为8名独立受试者。

method_function.text: 对提示措辞与示例顺序进行重复测量。

facts.statement: 附录给一个完整问答提示：角色为语言实验被试，四个非GP示例含两Yes两No，随后提供目标句与问题、以My answer is引出回答。主文还提到CoT尝试未显著改变结果，但未给详细独立结果表。

method_function.text: 保留输入包装、示例内容与输出接口。

facts.statement: 比较GPT系列、Llama3、Qwen2.5、Gemma2及OLMo1B/7B不同训练检查点，含基础版与既有指令版；本文描述的是选取模型/检查点做推断比较，没有将新训练写作正式实验步骤。主文检查点数量与附录清单不一致，见I001。

method_function.text: 把规模、已有训练阶段和模型版本作为比较维度。

facts.statement: 人类简单问题平均正确95.4%，GP问题37.0%；非GP、名词不适合作宾语、反身/非宾格动词通常有利于理解。合理材料GP/非GP差异仅接近显著，不能写所有条件都显著；及物倾向与准确率Pearson相关较弱（文中≤.19）。

method_function.text: 用分条件和词项关联检验多个解释，不仅报总分。

facts.statement: 人类显著性检验使用GLMM。表3合理/不合理子集写SentenceType+(1+SentenceType|SetId)，操纵比较写ManipulationType+(1+ManipulationType|SetId)；反身子集却印为SentenceType+(1+SetId)，缺分组竖线，原样保留为报告疑点。不能自动修成随机截距公式或补出participant随机项。

method_function.text: 保留按句集聚类与条件效应的模型设定。

facts.statement: 项目层人机相似度用Global Kendall Tau：跨条件取各项目人类平均正确率与模型平均正确答案概率的秩相关；条件层用Spearman关联六条件平均成绩的两个六维向量。聚合层次不同，不能互相替代或把相关当准确率。

method_function.text: 分别比较项目难度排序与条件难度排序。

facts.statement: 作者报告大模型通常在项目层与人类更相似，指令版对该相似度作用较小；OLMo7B随已有预训练检查点推进呈改善而1B未同样表现。条件层多数模型已较高相关，规模效应更弱；这些是模型比较关联，不证明训练规模单独造成行为机制变化。

method_function.text: 保留分层相似性结果及其解释边界。

facts.statement: 尽管人类与模型回答相同内容的理解问题，人类逐词限时而模型看到完整句子和问题。作者没有测眼动/阅读时；行为错误相似不能直接证明同样的增量解析机制或速度。

method_function.text: 约束跨系统比较的测量等价性和机制推断。

facts.statement: 改写任务排除OLMo1B/7B，让其他模型把句子拆成两句且保持同一情境；附录提示含四个句子与拆分示范并要求尽量简单。正确示例把狩猎者活动与鹿跑开分开，不新增错误宾语关系。

method_function.text: 换用生成性表达检验理解，不只问Yes/No。

facts.statement: 改写自动评分分三层：恰为两句的格式、目标动词仅出现在其中一句、潜在宾语名词不与该动词同句。前两项核对是否执行任务，第三项测目标理解；按前两指标不足90%过滤Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B后，剩余模型再报第三指标。过滤针对模型，不擅自改成逐响应删除。

method_function.text: 分离指令执行能力与理解质量，并明确过滤单位。

facts.statement: 改写中GP比非GP难；多数模型非GP准确率超过90%，GP内不合理宾语句通常最易。项目层用问答正确答案概率预测改写是否正确，以AUC评估，作者报告范围.595–.774、均值.696；这是跨任务分数区分能力，不是训练了新的预测器。

method_function.text: 用跨任务项目关联检查结论是否依赖问答形式。

facts.statement: Dall-e-3图像由人工分四类：正确（表达预期事件）；部分误解（包含GP误接关系但仍保留主句事件）；完全误解（主句事件缺失）；不适用（关键角色/元素缺失）。这四类不是把所有非正确图像一并计成GP误解。

method_function.text: 制定区分目标误解与一般生成失败的标注类别。

facts.statement: 图像结果展示正确/部分误解比例，部分误解在非GP及不合理名词条件较低，反身条件GP差较大。作者另尝试三个图像模型但质量不足未据此下结论；未把该探索记作成功跨模型验证。

method_function.text: 检查跨输出模态的目标误解模式并披露模型选择边界。

facts.statement: 因成本仅对模型开展改写和图像任务，人类改写支持来自既有文献而非本次新增样本；跨任务相似性支持对行为误解模式的检验，不构成同批人机多模态等价实验。

method_function.text: 限定多任务验证的样本来源和外推。

In this study, we explore object/subject GP sentences (similar to (1)) with humans and LLMs,
with both responding to exactly the same task,
namely, a comprehension question about the sentence (e.g., “Did the boy wash the dog?”). We
present three (non-mutually exclusive) hypotheses
regarding the challenges posed by GP sentences:
(a) Misinterpretation of the noun phrase as the object of the verb arises due to the difficulty of syntactic reanalysis; (b) Misinterpretation arises since
the noun phrase is a plausible object for the verb
(e.g., boys tend to wash dogs); (c) Misinterpretation arises since transitive verbs (“hunt”) entail
some object. Reflexive (“wash”) or unaccusative
(“drop”) verbs, which are interpreted with no direct object, will give rise to less misinterpretation.

Question: Did the man hunt the deer? Y/N
Note that the accurate answer to the question
above is “Not necessarily”. It is a possible interpretation of the sentence, and may be inferred
from it, but it is not entailed from the sentence. In
our experiments, as in previous experiments, we
consider "yes" to be a wrong answer here, whereas
"no" is considered the right answer.
Hypothesis 1: The GP syntax is hard. This
hypothesis suggests that misinterpretation occurs
because during incremental processing, the postverbal noun phrase (“the deer”) is first attached
as the object of the verb, requiring reanalysis when
the second verb is encountered. Often, the reanalysis is not complete, and the initial interpretation
lingers. According to this, reordering the clauses
(see Table 1) should improve accuracy by preventing initial misattachment.
Hypothesis 2: Readers attach the noun to
the first verb when it is a plausible object for
it. According to this hypothesis, readers interpret a noun as an object of a verb in the sentence
whenever this is semantically plausible, regardless of sentence position. If the noun is an implausible direct object, it will not be interpreted
as such, improving accuracy (see Table 1). Hypothesis 3: Readers search maximal interpretation of verb arguments. According to this hypothesis, optionally transitive verbs need objects
for full interpretation, so available nouns are taken
to fulfill this role. In contrast, alternating reflexive
(“wash”) and unaccusative verbs (“drop”) allow
complete interpretation intransitively, without an
object (e.g., The boy washed, The ball dropped),
Thus, such verb will allow more accurate interpretation than optionally transitive verbs (see Table 1). Note that for sentences such as "While the
boy washed the dog barked", the correct answer
for “Did the boy wash the dog?” is “No”. As for
the optionally transitive verbs, it can also be hypothesized that the tendency to interpret them as
taking an object depends on the verb’s transitivity bias (the probability that the verb appears with
a direct object). According to this, verbs with a
lower bias (e.g., “walk”) should lead to better accuracy compared to those with a higher bias (e.g.,

Materials In 45 sentences sets with optionally
transitive verbs (24 coming from Christianson
et al. (2001), 21 crafted for this study), we manipulated the structure of the sentence (GP or nonGP) and plausibility of the noun as the verb’s object (plausible or implausible), as exemplified in
(4). We also created 24 additional sets with reflexive/unaccusative verbs (12 from Christianson
et al. (2001) and 12 crafted for this study) in plausible sentences, manipulating structure (GP/nonGP), as exemplified in (5).
4.

5.

(a) GP, plausible: While the man hunted the deer ran
into the woods.
(b) Non-GP, plausible: The deer ran into the woods
while the man hunted.
(c) GP, implausible: While the man hunted the child
ran into the woods.
(d) Non-GP, implausible: The child ran into the
woods while the man hunted.
(a) GP, reflexive: While the boy washed the dog
barked loudly.
(b) Non-GP, reflexive: The dog barked loudly while
the boy washed.

To construct materials for the plausibility manipulation (hypothesis 2), we use insights from
Amouyal et al. (2024), and let GPT4 rate sentence
plausibility on a 1 to 7 scale. We select pairs where
the plausible sentence had a rating of at least 3
points higher than its implausible counterpart. For
the second part of hypothesis 3, we assessed each
optionally-transitive verb’s bias by its proportion
of transitive usages on Wikipedia. Our verbs’ bias
ranges from 0.102 (“sail”) to 0.775 (“explore”).
Appendix A lists the full estimated verb biases,
and all the sentences are in Appendix B.
For each sentence, we ask one of two questions:
1. Simple: “Did the deer run into the woods?”
2. GP: “Did the man hunt the deer?”
The simple question probes basic understanding of
the sentence, whereas the GP question targets the
potential misinterpretation.

Procedure Native English speakers were recruited via the Prolific platform.1 Sentences were
1

https://www.prolific.com/

displayed word-by-word, with each word shown
for 400ms and a 100ms blank screen between
words. After the sentence, the comprehension
question was presented for 5 seconds. If unanswered within this time, the response was marked
as incorrect. Participants completed two practice
items, followed by one experimental sentence and
one question. The single-trial design prevents fatigue (Christianson et al., 2022) and learning effects (Fine et al., 2013). Each of the 456 sentencequestion pair was shown to 10 participants. The
average completion time was 1:50 minutes, and
participants were compensated with 0.30£, equivalent to 9.64£ per hour. The experiment was approved by the Ethics Committee at Tel-Aviv University.

The accuracy on simple questions was high (average 95.4%, minimum 92.4%, maximum 98.7%).
Conversely, GP questions were much more challenging with an average accuracy of 37.0% on GP
questions.
Figure 1 (left) shows the average accuracy for
humans in the various conditions. As expected
from Hypothesis 1, accuracy is consistently higher
for non-GP structures. In addition, accuracy is
lower when the noun is a plausible direct object, indicating a tendency to interpret it as such
even without syntactic indication, supporting Hypothesis 2. The plausibility effect was more pronounced than the syntactic effect. In addition, accuracy was higher for GP sentences with a reflexive/unaccusative verb than for those with an optionally transitive verb, supporting Hypothesis 3,
and the effect of structure (GP vs. non-GP was
stronger for the former verbs).
We test statistical significance with Generalized
Linear Mixed-Effects Models (see Appendix C).
For Hypothesis 1, the difference between GP and
non-GP sentences was significant for implausible
(p = .019) and reflexive (p = 2.52e-13) sets, and
approached significance in the plausible sets, p
= .065. Hypothesis 2’s prediction was confirmed
with a significant difference between plausible and
implausible sentences (p = 4.11e-16). Hypothesis 3 is also supported with a significant difference
between reflexive/unaccusative verbs for both GP
sentences (p = 1.35e-5) and non-GP sentences (p
= 2.45e-14). The Pearson correlation between
transitivity bias and accuracy was weak (≤0.19)

To replicate the experiment with LLMs, we used
few-shot prompting, where each example includes
a sentence, a question, and the correct answer.2
The examples did not contain GP structures. Each
model was prompted 8 times, using two system
prompts and four example orderings. We extract the probabilities of the correct and incorrect answers tokens, averaging these across the 8
prompts. Appendix D shows an example prompt.
Models We test models from different families,
sizes and training checkpoints:

which did not lead to a signifnicant change in results.

1. GPT family (OpenAI, 2023): GPT-4, GPT4-Turbo, GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, o1-preview,
o1-mini.
2. Llama-3 (Grattafiori et al., 2024): All models from the Llama-3 family (Llama-3.2 and
Llama-3.1) available on HuggingFace.3
3. Qwen-2.5 (Yang et al., 2024; Qwen Team,
2024): All Qwen-2.5 models on HuggingFace except models of size 0.5b.
4. Gemma-2 (Team et al., 2024): All Gemma-2
models on HuggingFace.
5. Olmo (Groeneveld et al., 2024): 15 Olmo-1b
and Olmo-7b checkpoints along training.

These trends seem more pronounced for larger and
stronger models (the top two rows) compared to
smaller models (Olmo-1b).
Interestingly, LLM performance is not perfect
even for the strongest model, o1-preview, which
obtains an average accuracy of 78% (the secondstrongest model, Gemma-27B has an average accuracy of 74%). This far-from-perfect performance of LLMs is perhaps surprising since the entire sentence and question are presented in full to
the LLMs and there is no reason to suspect that
they should suffer from the same processing difficulties that humans do, especially those related to
the inability to overcome the initial misparse.

tion metric.4 We calculate a “Global” Kendall
Tau correlation by looking at all items in our data
(from all conditions) and comparing the average
accuracy of humans on those items to the average probability of the correct answer as provided
by the LLM, This measures whether the difficulty
ranking of all the items on our experiment is similar for humans and LLMs. Figure 4 presents the
findings for each model family.
Model size: As illustrated in Figure 4, larger
models exhibit a higher Kendall Tau correlation
with human judgements across all model families.
Instruction tuning: Instruction tuning appears
to have little impact on the similarity between humans and LLMs in this measure.
Pretraining tokens: In OLMo-7B, we see an increase in Kendall Tau correlation with the increase
in number of pretraining tokens. This pattern is
not observed in OLMo-1B, possibly because the
model is too weak to show significant effects.
We now move to analyzing the by-condition
correlation between humans and LLMs. Figure
5 shows the Spearman rank correlation between
humans and LLMs, comparing the average accuracy across the 6 conditions (correlating two vectors in R6 ). All models show a high Spearman
4
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kendall_rank_
correlation_coefficient. Our human data has a lot of
ranked ties, and Kendall Tau correlation accounts for ranked
ties contrary to Spearman rank correlation.

rank correlation with human data. This suggests
that models align well with humans in ranking average accuracy by sentence type, as opposed to a
global ranking across all items. Notably, model
size minimally impacts Spearman rank correlation
but significantly affects Kendall Tau, indicating
that larger models better differentiate item difficulty within conditions. In OLMo-7b, as training progresses, condition difficulty distinctions increasingly resemble humans’.

In addition to answering comprehension questions, we now test LLM understanding of GP sentences on two additional tasks – paraphraing and
text-to-image generation. Due to cost limitations,
we run this experiment on LLMs only. Patson
et al. (2009) performed a paraphrasing experiment
with humans using materials from Christianson
et al. (2001) and found that paraphrases showed
the same misinterpretations that comprehension
questions did.

We asked LLMs (excluding OLMo-1B and
OLMo-7B) to paraphrase a sentence by splitting
it into two parts. The correct answer would be to
change “While the man hunted the deer ran into
the woods.” into “The man hunted. The deer ran
into the woods.”. Using a few-shot prompt, we

provided examples of sentences and their breakdowns. The complete prompt is in Appendix F.
We automatically evaluated the paraphrases
using three metrics: a format metric (verifying that the paraphrase consistes of two sentences), a found-verb metric (ensuring that the
verb “hunted” appears in just one sentence), and
a correct-paraphrase metric (checking that the
noun “deer” does not appear in the same sentence as “hunted”). The first two metrics check
if the model correctly executed the paraphrasing
task, while the last evaluates sentence comprehension. Models that scored below 90% accuracy
in the format and found-verb metrics (Qwen2.51.5B, Qwen2.5-3B) were filtered out, and for the
remaining models we measured performance with
the correct-paraphrase metric.

Figure 6 shows the average accuracy across
for our model families, categorized by sentence
type. We observe that GP sentences are universally more challenging to paraphrase for all models and sentence types. For almost all LLMs, the
accuracy on the non-GP sentences is above 90%
across all the manipulations. Moreover, among
the GP sentences, implausible ones have the highest paraphrase accuracy across models. Sentences
like “The man hunted the child.” seem to be too
out of distribution for our LLMs to generate.
We also performed an item-level analysis,
where we checked whether the probability assigned to the correct answer for the GP question
predicts correct paraphrasing. We measure the

AUC for the probability assigned to the correct answer, and find that all our models have an AUC
over 0.5, with the minimal AUC being 0.595, the
maximal 0.774 and the average 0.696. This suggests that the probability of correctly answering
the GP question can strongly predict whether paraphrasing will be accurate. Instruction tuning and
model sizes had little effect on the AUC.

We asked Dall-e-3 (OpenAI, 2024)5 to generate
images for our experimental sentences and manually categorized the resulting images into four
groups: “correctly understood”, where the image accurately depicts the intended meaning of
the sentence, e.g., in “while the man hunted the
deer ran into the woods”, the image would depict a man hunting, and a deer running; “partial
misunderstanding”, where the image reflects the
misinterpretation suggested by the garden path,
namely, in the above example, a man hunting a
5
We tried 3 other text-to-image models to generate images
but the results were not good enough to draw any conclusion.

deer, and a deer running; “complete misunderstanding”, where the interpretation of the main
clause is absent, namely for the example above,
the image would not depict a deer running; and
“not applicable”, where some elements of the
sentence are missing, e.g. in the example above
there would either be no man, or no deer. Figure 7
provides examples for each category.

Figure 8 shows the proportion of the correctly understood and partially understood classes.
Looking at the partial-misunderstanding label,
which corresponds to the type of misinterpretation
we have been investigating, we see trends that are
similar to the comprehension questions case. The
proportion of examples with this label is lower for
non-GP than for GP sentences and for sentences
with implausible compared to plausible nouns. In
addition, the gap between GP and non-GP sentences is larger for the reflexive/unaccusative case.
This further supports the empirical results we saw
for comprehension questions and paraphrasing.

Limitations
In our study, we evaluated reading comprehension
across a wide array of LLMs. However, the latest
state-of-the-art models appeared too late to be incorporated into this version of our paper. Assessing their understanding of our sets would be interesting for a future version of this paper. Additionally, our focus was limited to measuring reading
comprehension on Subject/Object GP sentences.
Exploring LLMs’ comprehension of other types of
GP sentences would also be interesting. Finally,
we did not collect data on metrics beyond reading
comprehension, such as eye gaze or reading time,
in our experiments. Gathering such metrics and
analyzing their correlation with sentence comprehension could provide valuable insights.
